title: Plague years
hookLine: during the plague, he fled his home with his family and admired the calm of peasants facing death (Essays 3.12)

cards: The plague reached the country around Montaigne's house. He writes about it in book three, in an essay called Of physiognomy. He gathered his family and left home, looking for somewhere safe.
It wasn't easy: a family fleeing the plague frightened the people they hoped would take them in. Friends grew wary; hosts grew nervous at any sign of illness.
The man who wrote so calmly about death in his tower now faced it on the road, with his household behind him. And what he noticed most, he says, wasn't the scholars. It was the farmers.

teach.b: First, what he saw. The country people faced the sickness, he writes, with a plainness that stunned him. The grapes were left hanging on the vines as people readied themselves for death without drama.
He tells of a man, still healthy, already digging his own grave, and of others who lay down in theirs while still alive. Grim pictures, but what struck him was the quiet in them.
Second, calm without books. Montaigne had spent a long time reading philosophers on how to prepare for death. These people had read none of it, and met death more steadily than the learned.
He doesn't romanticize their hardship; he's honest that their calm wasn't borrowed from a library. Third, nature as teacher.
If you don't know how to die, he writes, roughly, don't worry: nature will teach you fully when the moment comes.
Then a line that turns it around: we trouble our life with worry about death, and our death with worry about life. Fourth, plain and brave.
The title points to faces, and he spends much of the essay on Socrates, whose face was plain, even ugly by his account, and whose courage was not.
No show, no speech, just steadiness. The bravest person you know may not be the loudest.
And if thoughts of death weigh on you now, you don't have to hold them alone: in the US you can call or text 988, and wherever you are, local emergency help is there.

how: Readers of Montaigne's essay Of physiognomy often remember his account of the plague, and his admiration for country people who met death with a calm no book had taught them.

games.q: you're Montaigne, the plague is close, and you've read the philosophers on death. who teaches you most?
games.why: the country people, who met death plainly without the books, struck him more than anything he'd read.

practice: Bring to mind someone who carried something hard without making a show of it: a grandparent, a nurse, a friend who kept going through an illness or a loss.
Remember one ordinary thing they did in the middle of it, making tea, going to work, telling a joke, and let that small, steady act be your teacher for these minutes.

wordCard.voice: Plague years. Montaigne on the road, learning steadiness from people who had read none of the books he had. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the peasants' calm. A week with Montaigne: the whole human condition, steady change, three companies, a new route, two not one, not so sure, and the peasants' calm. That's the week.
